items.caption: Listens in on the internal Samsung NASA bus (RS485, F1/F2 connection) and reads the status values that are exchanged there anyway -- without internet, without an account, without Samsung's official Modbus accessory module MIM-B19N. Details: https://github.com/DG65/NRGSamsungEhs

Steps: 1. Connect an RS485-to-Ethernet adapter to the F1/F2 connection of the heat pump (see help below) → 2. Enter its IP address and port → 3. Apply → 4. Switch on "SamsungEhs active" and apply again.

Which adapter do I need and how do I connect it?

popup.caption: Which adapter do I need and how do I connect it?

items.caption: A simple RS485-to-Ethernet adapter (e.g. a Waveshare module or an Elfin EW11) is enough -- connected to the F1/F2 connection of the heat pump (the internal bus between outdoor and indoor unit). No original Samsung accessory is needed. The adapter has to pass the serial data stream through 1:1 over a TCP connection ("transparent bridge"/"serial to TCP") and must not translate anything itself. IP address and port are then those of the adapter, not of the heat pump itself.
Why a listening window instead of a direct query?

popup.caption: Why a listening window instead of a direct query?

items.caption: Unlike Modbus, SamsungEhs does not query individual values -- the outdoor and indoor unit exchange status values on the NASA bus all the time anyway. The module therefore listens for a few seconds in every cycle and takes over what passes by in that time. A window that is too short can miss individual values (they then simply stay at their last known state). Values above about 30 s can fail on some Symcon installations because of the script execution time (kernel settings) -- this only affects the single cycle, no data is lost. A listening window close to the update interval lengthens the actual cycle accordingly (the module always waits for the recording to finish, even if the timer would be due again).
